title: HTML Documents and Semantic Elements
summary: Write pages that browsers, search engines, and screen readers understand, from the head to text, links, images, and landmarks.
intro: HTML is the part of a page everything else stands on. CSS styles it, JavaScript changes it, search engines read it to decide what your page is about, and screen readers read it aloud to people who can't see the screen. Get it right, and a page works for all of them before you add a single style. Get it wrong, and you'll see pages that look tiny on phones, show garbled letters, share as a blank link preview, or make no sense read aloud. This lesson teaches you to write HTML well: how elements and attributes work, the lines every page starts with, and the elements for text, links, pictures, and the regions of a page, each chosen for what it means. You'll build pages for a small bakery as you go.

steps.title: Elements, tags, and attributes
steps.body:
Every page is built from elements, and every element follows the same few rules. Learn them once, and you can read the HTML of any page, including the source of sites you visit every day. ## Elements and tags An **element** is one piece of a page: a heading, a paragraph, a link, a picture. Most elements are written as a **start tag**, then the content, then an **end tag**: ```html

Bread is best on the day it's baked.

``` `

` is the start tag, and `

`, with a slash, is the end tag. Together with the text between them, they make one paragraph element. Tag names don't care about capital letters, but everyone writes them in lowercase. ## Nesting Elements go inside other elements. That's called **nesting**, and it's what gives the DOM its tree shape. Each element has to close inside the element it opened in, like boxes packed inside boxes: ```html

Bake it for 40 minutes, then let it cool.

``` `` opens inside the paragraph and closes inside it too. Writing `

` before `` would close the boxes in the wrong order, and the parser would have to guess what you meant. ## Void elements A few elements can't hold anything, so they have no end tag. These are the **void elements**. The ones you'll use most are `` for a picture, `` for a form field, `
` for a line break, `
` for a dividing line, and `` and `` in the head. You'll also see them written with a slash, like `
`, in older code and in React. In HTML that slash is allowed, and it does nothing. ## Attributes **Attributes** give an element extra information. They go inside the start tag: a name, an equals sign, and a value in double quotes. An element can have several, separated by spaces, in any order: ```html ``` `src` says which picture file to show, and `alt` describes it in words, for anyone who can't see it. The images part explains both. Some attributes are simply on or off. These are **boolean attributes**, and being there at all means on: `` makes a field you can't type in. That leads to a classic mistake: `disabled="false"` still disables the field, because the browser only checks whether the attribute is there. To turn it off, leave it out. ## Global attributes Most attributes belong to one kind of element, like `src` to pictures. A few work on any element. They're called **global attributes**: - `id` gives the element a name that's unique on the page. Links can jump to it, and scripts can find it. - `class` gives it one or more group names, separated by spaces, like `class="price sale"`. Many elements can share a class, and CSS uses classes to pick which elements to style. - `lang` names the language of its text, like `lang="fr"` for French, so a screen reader pronounces it right. - `hidden` is a boolean that hides the element completely, as if it weren't drawn at all. - `data-` attributes hold your own information for scripts to read, with any name you like after the dash, like `data-price="3.50"`. ## Comments `` ends it. Comments are notes for people reading the code, and the browser doesn't show them. They're still sent to everyone, though, and View Page Source shows them, so never put anything private in one. ## Spaces, and characters with a job Two rules catch out everyone new to HTML. First, HTML collapses **whitespace**: spaces, tabs, and line breaks in a row all show as one space. So you can indent your code and break lines wherever you like, and the page looks the same. A blank line doesn't start a new paragraph. A new `

` does. Second, two characters have jobs. `<` starts a tag, and `&` starts a **character reference**, a short code that stands for one character. To show them as text, write `<` for `<` and `&` for `&`. Two more are handy: `"` puts a double quote inside an attribute's value, and ` ` is a space that never breaks a line, for things like `10 km`. Other characters, like é, €, or an emoji, you can just type, once the page says it uses UTF-8, which the next part sets up. ## Checking your HTML As the previous lesson showed, the parser never stops at a mistake. It guesses, and carries on. To find mistakes before it has to guess, use a **validator**, a program that checks a page against the HTML standard. The W3C runs a free one at [validator.w3.org/nu](https://validator.w3.org/nu/): paste in your HTML, or give it an address, and it lists every problem with its line number. Here's a page with two mistakes on lines 9 and 10, which the example below checks: ```html My recipes

My recipes

Bread, slowly

```

examples.title: A page with every kind of attribute
examples.prompt: In the Playground, make a folder called `bakery` and save this in it as `index.html`. Start Python's server in the folder and open `http://localhost:8000/`.
examples.code:
Mia's Bakery

Bread, cakes & coffee, baked every morning.

Try our pain au chocolat.

Sourdough loaf: 3.50

Closed for the holidays.
examples.explanation: You'll see the heading, then Bread, cakes & coffee, baked every morning, on one line with single spaces, since whitespace collapses. The comment doesn't show, and neither does the paragraph with `hidden`. `<span>` is an element with no meaning of its own, used here only to mark the French words with `lang`. The `id`, the classes, and `data-price` change nothing you can see: they're there for links, CSS, and scripts. There's no `loaf.jpg` in the folder yet, so the browser shows the `alt` text in its place, and the server's terminal shows a 404 for it. The first lines, from `<!doctype html>` to `<body>`, are the skeleton the next part explains.

examples.title: Checking a page with the validator
examples.prompt: Save the page with two mistakes as `mistakes.html` in `bakery`, then send it to the validator from the Playground's terminal. `-H` adds a header saying it's HTML, and `--data-binary @mistakes.html` sends the file as the request's body.
examples.output:
:9.21-9.24: error: End tag “p” seen, but there were open elements.
:9.11-9.14: error: Unclosed element “em”.
:9.25-9.29: error: No “em” element in scope but a “em” end tag seen.
:10.1-10.20: error: An “img” element must have an “alt” attribute, except under certain conditions. For details, consult guidance on providing text alternatives for images.
examples.explanation: Each line of the answer starts with where the problem is: `9.21-9.24` means line 9, characters 21 to 24. The first three errors are one mistake, the end tags in the wrong order, seen from three sides. The last one is a picture with no `alt`. `?out=gnu` in the address asks for this short format, one problem per line. Sending a file with curl like this is a POST request with a body, the kind of request the previous lessons described. The validator's web page does the same when you paste HTML into it.

steps.title: The document skeleton and the head
steps.body:
The first dozen lines of nearly every page are the same, and none of them show on the page. They tell the browser how to read the page, tell phones how wide to draw it, tell search engines what it's about, and tell chat apps what to show when someone shares the link. Leave one out, and something breaks in a place you might not think to look. ## The skeleton Here's the start of a page for the bakery, with everything a real page's head usually holds: ```html Sourdough Loaf | Mia's Bakery

Sourdough Loaf

``` ## The doctype `` always comes first. It isn't a tag: it tells the browser to follow today's rules. Without it, browsers switch to **quirks mode**, where they copy the mistakes of browsers from the late 1990s so that very old pages still look the way they did. Sizes, spacing, and tables come out differently, and your CSS won't do what the lessons say. Chrome warns you about it in the Issues tab of DevTools. ## html, head, and body `` holds everything, and its `lang` attribute names the page's language. Screen readers use it to choose a voice and pronunciation, browsers use it to offer translation, and search engines use it to match the page with readers. Inside are two parts. `` holds information about the page, and `` holds what's on it. The parser would add all three if you left them out, as the previous lesson showed, but write them anyway: it's clearer, and `lang` needs a home. ## The character set `` says how the page's letters are stored as bytes. It belongs at the top of the head, since the browser looks for it in the first 1,024 bytes. Without it, and without a charset in the server's `Content-Type` header, the browser has to guess, and accented letters come out garbled. The example below shows it happening. ## The viewport Phones have small screens, and many old sites were built for wide ones. So without being told otherwise, a phone lays a page out as if its screen were 980 pixels wide, then shrinks the whole thing down to fit, leaving the text too small to read. `` tells it to lay the page out at the phone's own width, at normal size. Every page needs it. The CSS lessons build on it to make one page fit every screen. ## The title and the description The `` is the page's name. It shows on the browser tab, in bookmarks and history, and as the blue headline in search results, and it's the first thing a screen reader says. Make it specific to the page, and put the page's own subject first: Sourdough Loaf | Mia's Bakery, not Home. `<meta name="description">` is a sentence or two about the page. Search engines often show it under the title in their results, so it's your chance to say why someone should click. A `<meta>` element is how the head holds information like this: a `name` saying what it is, and its `content`. ## Links to other files `<link>` connects the page to another file. Its `rel` attribute, short for relationship, says how. `rel="stylesheet"` loads CSS. `rel="icon"` names the **favicon**, the small picture on the browser tab. Without one, browsers ask for `/favicon.ico` on their own, which is why your server's terminal may have shown a 404 for it. `<script>` loads JavaScript. The `defer` attribute lets the parser carry on while the script downloads, and runs it once the page is read. The JavaScript lessons explain it. Note that `<script>` always needs its end tag, even with nothing between the tags. ## Link previews When you paste a link into a chat app or a social site, it fetches the page and builds a preview card from it: a title, a line of text, and a picture. It finds them in the **Open Graph** tags, the `<meta>` lines whose `property` starts with `og:`. The name comes from Facebook, which created them, but nearly every app reads them now. `og:image` needs a full address, with `https://` and the host, since the app reads it from somewhere else. ```diagram html-documents-head-readers Every line in the head is there for someone, and most of them aren't people. ```

steps.title: Text, headings, and lists
steps.body:
Most of a page is text, and HTML has an element for each job text does: a heading, a quote, a step in a recipe. Choosing the one that matches the meaning is what lets a screen reader jump straight to the part you want, and lets a search engine tell what your page is about. ## Paragraphs and headings `

` is a paragraph. Headings come in six levels, `

` to `

`, and they work like the outline of a document: - `

` is the page's main heading, and a page has one. - `

` starts each main section, `

` a part inside an `

` section, and so on down. - Don't skip a level, like an `

` straight after an `

`. The levels are the outline, so a gap looks like a missing section. Pick a heading by its level in the outline, never by how big it looks. CSS can make any heading any size. People using screen readers move around a page by its headings more than any other way, listening to the list of them and jumping to the one they want, so the outline has to make sense on its own. ## Importance, stress, and other voices Four elements look alike in the browser's default styles, but mean different things: - `` is for importance or urgency: **Contains nuts.** It shows in bold. - `` is for stress that changes what a sentence means, the word you'd say louder: we *do* open on Sundays. It shows in italics. - `` draws attention without adding importance, like the product names in a review. It shows in bold. - `` is for words in a different voice, like a word from another language or a term being defined. It shows in italics. When you only want bold or italic looks, with no meaning, use CSS instead. ## Code, quotes, and times - `` marks a piece of code, like a file name or a command. It shows in a fixed-width font, where every letter is as wide as the next. - `
`, for preformatted, keeps every space and line break exactly as you typed it. It's the one exception to whitespace collapsing, and the usual home for a whole block of code, written as `
`.
- `
` holds a quotation of a paragraph or more, and its `cite` attribute can give the address it came from.
- `` marks a date or a time, and its `datetime` attribute writes it in a form computers read for certain: `Saturday the 21st`. Search engines and calendar apps read it.

## Lists

HTML has three kinds of list:

- `
    `, an **unordered list**, is a list where the order doesn't matter, like a set of ingredients. Browsers show a bullet before each item.
- `
      `, an **ordered list**, is a list where the order matters, like the steps of a recipe. Browsers number the items.
- `
      `, a **description list**, pairs terms with what they mean, like a glossary or a product's details. Each term goes in `
      ` and its meaning in `
      `.

The items of `
        ` and `
          ` each go in an `
        1. `, a list item. A list can go inside an `
        2. ` to make a list within a list. Site menus are usually a `
            ` of links, since they're a list of places, and that's how screen readers announce them: a list of five items.

## Block and inline

You've seen that a paragraph starts on a new line while `` sits inside a line of text. That comes from the user agent stylesheet, the browser's own default styles from the previous lesson:

- **Block** elements start on a new line and stretch across the full width available: `
            `, the headings, the lists and their items, `
            `, and `
            `.
- **Inline** elements sit inside a line of text and take only the room their content needs: ``, ``, ``, ``, and ``.

Two elements mean nothing at all, for when no other element fits. `
            ` is a block with no meaning, used to group things for styling. `` is its inline twin. Reach for them last, after you've checked that no element with a meaning fits.

## Choose by meaning

The rule behind this whole part is to choose an element for what its content is, and let CSS decide how it looks. A bulleted look isn't a reason to use `
              `, but a list of things is. Big text isn't a reason to use `
              `, but the start of a section is. When the meaning is right, the page works in every browser, in every screen reader, and in search engines, whatever your CSS does.

examples.title: A recipe page
examples.prompt: Save this in `bakery` as `recipe.html` and open it. Then open DevTools, find the `ol` in the Elements tab, and look at its `display` in the Computed pane.
examples.code:
Sourdough Loaf

Posted 21 November 2026. Contains wheat.

Ingredients

  • 500 g strong white flour
  • 350 g water
  • 100 g starter
  • 10 g salt

Method

  1. Mix everything, then leave it for at least 12 hours.
  2. Shape the dough and let it rise.
  3. Bake at 230°C for 40 minutes.

Details

Makes
One loaf
Keeps
Three days in a paper bag

The best bread in town.
examples.explanation: The page shows one main heading and three sections, each with an `<h2>`. The ingredients have bullets, the method's steps are numbered 1 to 3, and the details show each term with its description indented below it. None of that came from your CSS, since there isn't any: it's all the browser's defaults. The Computed pane shows `display: block` for the `ol`, the user agent stylesheet's doing. Open the `time` and you'll find `display: inline`. A screen reader would announce three headings, a list of four items, and a list of three, and someone listening could jump straight to Method.

steps.title: Links and the addresses in them
steps.body:
Links are what make the web a web. Every link holds an address, and the lessons on how the web works showed you how addresses are built and how a relative path is filled in. This part puts that to work in pages, and adds the attributes that change where a link goes and what it does. ## The a element A link is an `` element, short for anchor, and its `href` attribute holds the address: ```html

See all our breads.

``` The text between the tags is what people click, and what screen readers read out when they list a page's links. So make it say where it goes: all our breads, not click here. A list of ten links all called click here tells a listener nothing. ## Three ways to write the address An `href` can be any of the three kinds of address from the first lessons: - **Absolute**, with a scheme and a host: `https://example.com/about.html`. Use it for other sites. - **Root-relative**, starting with `/`: `/contact.html` starts at the root of this site, whichever page it's on. - **Relative**, with no `/` at the start: `cake.html` or `../index.html` start from the folder the current page is in. ```diagram html-documents-links Each link on the bread page, and the file it leads to. ``` In the diagram, the page `/recipes/bread.html` has five links. `cake.html` is next to it in the `recipes` folder. `images/loaf.jpg` is in a folder inside that one. `../index.html` goes up one folder to the home page. `/contact.html` starts from the root, so it lands in the same place from any page. And `#method` stays on the same page. Within your own site, root-relative addresses are the easiest to get right, since they mean the same thing on every page. Relative ones are handy for files that always travel together, like a page and its own pictures. ## Jumping to a spot on a page A link to a **fragment** jumps to an element on a page: `href="#method"` scrolls to the element whose `id` is `method`, on this same page. `href="recipes/bread.html#method"` opens that page, then scrolls. As the first lessons showed, the fragment never reaches the server, so jumping around a page you already have is instant. That makes contents lists easy. Give each `

` an `id`, and link to each one from a list at the top. ## Opening a new tab `target="_blank"` opens the link in a new tab. Use it rarely, since people can open a new tab themselves when they want one, and a page that opens tabs on its own takes that choice away. It suits links that would interrupt something, like the terms and conditions while someone is filling in a form. You'll often see `rel="noopener"` next to it. Years ago, a page opened this way could take control of the tab that opened it, and send it somewhere else while you weren't looking. `noopener` stops that. Browsers now do this by default for every `target="_blank"` link, but the attribute is still everywhere in real code, and it does no harm. ## Downloads, email, and phone numbers - `download` makes the browser save the file instead of showing it: `Download the menu`. It only works for files on your own site. - `mailto:` in place of `https:` opens an email to that address: `href="mailto:hello@bakery.example.com"`. - `tel:` dials a number on a phone: `href="tel:+441130000000"`. Write the number in full, with its country code and no spaces. ## Links go places, buttons do things A link and a button can look the same, but they have different jobs. A link **goes somewhere**: it has an address, so people can open it in a new tab, copy it, or bookmark it. A `

examples.prompt: Make a `recipes` folder inside `bakery`, save this there as `bread.html`, and open `http://localhost:8000/recipes/bread.html`. Hover over each link and read the full address at the bottom corner of the browser window.

Mix, wait, shape, wait, bake.
examples.explanation: Hovering shows the address each `href` turns into. `cake.html` becomes `http://localhost:8000/recipes/cake.html`, `../index.html` becomes `http://localhost:8000/index.html`, and `/contact.html` becomes `http://localhost:8000/contact.html`. The first link becomes `http://localhost:8000/recipes/bread.html#method`, and clicking it scrolls to Method without asking the server for anything: no new line appears in its terminal. To make the MDN link open a new tab, add `target="_blank"` to it. The email link opens your email app, if you have one set up.

steps.title: Pictures, video, and sound
steps.body: Pictures are usually the biggest files on a page, and the most likely to go wrong. They can load slowly, push text around as they arrive, or mean nothing to someone who can't see them. A few attributes fix all three, and let each visitor's browser pick the right size of picture for their screen. ## The img element ```html ``` `src` is the picture's address. `alt` is its **alternative text**: what a screen reader reads out in its place, and what the browser shows if the picture can't load. Describe what the picture is there to say, in a short sentence. A picture that's only decoration, like a swirl in a corner, gets an empty `alt=""`, so screen readers skip it. Never leave `alt` out: without it, many screen readers read out the file name instead. `width` and `height` give the picture's real size in pixels. The browser needs them to save the right amount of room before the picture arrives. Without them, layout gives the picture no room at first, then shoves the text down when it loads: the layout shift from the previous lesson. With them, the browser works out the shape in advance. CSS can still make the picture any size, and the shape is kept. ## The right size for each screen A phone doesn't need the huge picture a wide screen does, and sending it anyway wastes the visitor's time and data. `srcset` offers the browser several sizes of the same picture, and `sizes` tells it how wide the picture will show: ```html ``` Each entry in `srcset` is a file and its width in pixels, with a `w` after it. `sizes` reads: on a screen at least 800 pixels wide, the picture fills half the width of the viewport (`50vw`, half the viewport's width), and on anything smaller, all of it (`100vw`). The browser also knows the screen's **pixel density**. Many screens pack two or three tiny pixels into each pixel CSS counts, so text and pictures look sharp. On those, a picture needs two or three times as many pixels to look crisp. So the browser multiplies the width the picture will show at by the density, and picks the smallest file at least that wide. ```diagram html-documents-srcset The same three files, and the one each screen picks. ``` ## Newer formats, with a fallback **AVIF** and **WebP** are newer picture formats that make files much smaller than JPEG at the same quality. `` lets you offer them, with a JPEG for any browser that can't show them: ```html ``` The browser takes the first `` whose `type`, a media type from the first lessons, it can show. The `` is always needed: it's what's actually drawn, and where `alt` lives. ## Loading in the right order - `loading="lazy"` waits to fetch a picture until it's near the part of the page on screen. Use it for pictures further down the page, and never for the main one at the top. - `fetchpriority="high"` asks the browser to fetch a picture before other files, for the big one at the top that people see first. It's Baseline Newly available, and browsers without it simply ignore it. ## Captions, video, and sound `

examples.title: A figure with a caption, and a video
examples.prompt: Two pieces of a bakery page: a photo with a caption, and a short video with captions. Each file name stands for a file in the site's `images` and `media` folders.
examples.explanation: The photo is further down the page, so it loads lazily, and its `width` and `height` keep its space ready either way. Its `alt` says what's in it, while the caption, which everyone sees, adds something the photo can't. The video shows the browser's controls, and `poster` is the picture shown before it plays. The browser takes the first `<source>` it can play: WebM if it can, MP4 if not. `<track>` offers English captions, which people turn on from the player's menu. `srclang` names their language, and `label` is the name shown in that menu.

steps.title: Landmarks and the accessibility tree
steps.body:
A screen reader can't see your layout. It doesn't know the menu is at the top or the main story is in the middle, unless your HTML says so. The elements in this part do, and they build something you can't see but should check on every page you make: the accessibility tree.

## Landmarks

Most pages have the same few regions: a header with the site's name, a menu, the main content, perhaps a sidebar, and a footer. HTML has an element for each one:

- `<header>`: the top of the page, usually with the site's name and menu.
- `<nav>`: a group of links for getting around the site.
- `<main>`: the page's own content, the reason it exists. A page has one.
- `<aside>`: something to one side, related but not essential, like a list of other recipes.
- `<footer>`: the bottom of the page, with contact details and small print.
- `<section>`: one part of the content, with a heading of its own.
- `<article>`: a piece that would make sense alone, like a blog post, a review, or a news story.

Screen readers call these regions **landmarks**, and list them, so people can jump straight to the main content or the menu instead of listening to the whole page from the top. A page built only from `<div>` elements has none.

## The accessibility tree

From the DOM, the browser builds a second tree, the **accessibility tree**. It's what screen readers and other **assistive technology**, the tools people use in place of a screen, a mouse, or a keyboard, read instead of the DOM. Each node in it has three things:

- A **role**: what it is, like a link, a button, a heading at level 2, or the main landmark.
- A **name**: what it's called, taken from its text, its `alt`, or its label.
- A **state**: anything that changes, like checked, expanded, or disabled.

```diagram html-documents-a11y-tree
Each element with a meaning becomes a node with a role and a name.
```

A `<div>` with no meaning shows up as nothing, and its contents are passed up to the node above. That's why a clickable `<div>` fails: its node has no role saying it can be clicked.

To see the tree, open the Elements tab in DevTools, click an element, and choose the **Accessibility** pane beside the tree. It shows that element's role, name, and state.

## ARIA, and its first rule

**ARIA**, short for Accessible Rich Internet Applications, is a set of attributes that change the accessibility tree: `role` sets a role, `aria-label` sets a name, and attributes like `aria-expanded` set a state. They change only what assistive technology is told, never what the element does.

So ARIA's own first rule is to not use it when an HTML element already does the job. `<div role="button">` tells a screen reader it's a button, but it still can't be reached with Tab, and Enter does nothing, until you write JavaScript for all of that. `<button>` does it all already. Use real elements first, and ARIA only for what HTML has no element for.

## Built-in pieces that open and close

Three things that used to need JavaScript are now plain HTML, with the right roles and keyboard controls built in:

- `<details>` with a `<summary>` inside makes a section that opens and closes when you click its summary, like a question in a list of questions.
- `<dialog>` is a box that appears over the page and asks for attention, like a message asking whether you're sure. Opening it takes a line of JavaScript, which the JavaScript lessons show.
- The `popover` attribute turns an element into a small panel that shows over the page, and closes when you click elsewhere or press Esc. A button with `popovertarget` set to the panel's `id` opens it, with no script at all.

## Tables, for tables

`<table>` is for **tabular data**: information in rows and columns, like opening hours or prices. Long ago, people used tables to lay out whole pages, and screen readers still read every one as a grid, so a table used for layout makes nonsense read aloud. CSS does layout now. For a real table:

- `<caption>` gives the table a title.
- `<th>` is a header cell, and `scope="col"` or `scope="row"` says whether it heads a column or a row.
- `<td>` is an ordinary cell, and `<tr>` is a row.

With headers marked, a screen reader can say Saturday, opens, 7 a.m. for each cell, not just 7 a.m.

Pages also need a way to send things back, like an order or a search. The next lesson covers forms.

examples.title: A page with landmarks, and its tree
examples.prompt: Save this in `bakery` as `home.html` and open it. Then open DevTools, and in the Elements tab click the Accessibility pane's option to show the full-page accessibility tree.
examples.code:
Mia's Bakery
  • Breads
  • Cakes

Fresh bread daily

We bake from 5 a.m., so it's warm when we open.

Opening hours

Every day but Monday, 7 a.m. to 3 p.m.

12 Mill Lane, Leeds
examples.explanation: The page looks plain, since landmarks have no look of their own. Click Opening hours and the details open, with no script. The accessibility tree shows what a screen reader gets: a banner landmark (the role of the page's `<header>`) holding the Mia's Bakery link and a navigation landmark with a list of two links, then the main landmark with a level 1 heading, the paragraph, and a group holding a disclosure triangle named Opening hours, marked as not expanded until you open it. Last comes a contentinfo landmark, the footer's role. Every role came from choosing the right element. There isn't a single ARIA attribute on the page.

recap:
- Elements nest inside each other and close in order, and void elements like img and input have no end tag.
- Attributes add information to an element, and a boolean attribute is on whenever it's there at all.
- Every page needs the doctype, html with lang, meta charset first, the viewport line, and a specific title.
- Choose elements for what their content means, and let CSS decide how it looks.
- Write link text that says where the link goes, and use links to go places and buttons to do things.
- Give every picture alt text, plus width and height so the page doesn't jump when it loads.
- srcset and sizes let each screen pick the smallest picture that will still look sharp.
- Landmarks and native elements build the accessibility tree that screen readers use, with no ARIA needed.
